drills.q: A pod shows CrashLoopBackOff with an empty kubectl logs output. What's your next command and why?
drills.a: kubectl logs <pod> --previous — the currently running instance may be mid-crash-loop with nothing logged yet, but --previous retrieves the last terminated instance's output, which almost always has the real error.

drills.q: describe pod shows Last State Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137. Your teammate wants to immediately double the memory limit. What do you check first?
drills.a: container_memory_working_set_bytes history over hours/days — a steadily climbing line indicates a genuine leak that a bigger limit only delays, while a bounded spike justifies a limit increase. Raising the limit without checking first can mask a leak.

drills.q: An entire node's pods start hitting ImagePullBackOff right after a large scale-up event, while other nodes are fine. Diagnose.
drills.a: Registry rate limiting hit during a burst of simultaneous pulls on that node — Events will show a 429-flavored error. Fix by authenticating pulls or running an in-cluster pull-through cache/mirror to absorb burst pulls.

drills.q: A fleet-wide CrashLoopBackOff starts immediately after a deploy. What's your first action, before reading any logs?
drills.a: Roll back (kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>) first, diagnose after — restoring service takes priority mid-incident, and the previous working ReplicaSet is a fast, low-risk revert compared to live debugging while users are impacted.

drills.q: After the rollback in the previous scenario, replicas keep crash-looping even on the old, previously-stable image. What does this tell you?
drills.a: It's probably not the deploy itself — something else changed at the same timestamp (a database migration that already ran and can't be un-run, a rotated secret/config, an independently changed downstream dependency). Investigate what else changed concurrently, not the image.

drills.q: A pod keeps failing its liveness probe and getting killed with exit code 0, but the app has no obvious bug. What's a resourcing-related explanation, and how would you confirm it?
drills.a: Severe CPU throttling (CFS quota exhaustion) can starve the app of CPU time badly enough that it can't respond to the probe within its timeout, producing what looks like a probe-tuning issue. Confirm by correlating container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total spikes against the probe failure timestamps.

drills.q: External API calls from in-cluster services show a steady, not intermittent, latency overhead compared to calls made from outside the cluster. DNS 'works fine.' Diagnose.
drills.a: ndots:5 default causing search-domain expansion — every external name with fewer than 5 dots is tried against cluster search domains first, generating several wasted NXDOMAIN queries before the absolute name succeeds. Fix with a trailing-dot FQDN or a lower ndots value via dnsConfig.options.

drills.q: Some external DNS lookups from pods intermittently hang for exactly ~5 seconds before succeeding. Restarting CoreDNS doesn't help. What's actually happening?
drills.a: A kernel-level conntrack race: two near-simultaneous UDP DNS queries (typically A and AAAA) from the same source port can collide during conntrack table insertion, dropping one packet; the resolver waits out its full timeout. It's not a CoreDNS issue — mitigate by forcing TCP DNS or disabling unnecessary AAAA lookups.

drills.q: A distroless production image with no shell needs live debugging. What's the modern approach, and what does it share with the target container?
drills.a: kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> — injects a temporary ephemeral container sharing the target's network namespace and, via --target, its process namespace, without modifying the pod spec or restarting it. GA since Kubernetes 1.25.

drills.q: A node shows a burst of Evicted pods across several unrelated Deployments, none of which individually show high memory usage. What should you check on the node itself, and why might this happen?
drills.a: Node-level disk usage (nodefs/imagefs) via kubectl debug node/<name> -it --image=busybox -- chroot /host sh — a high-volume logger from one unrelated pod can fill node disk and trigger disk-pressure eviction that removes pods in QoS order regardless of whether they caused the pressure ('innocent bystander' pattern).
